newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Capital curbs worst case option -- Bnk Negara's Zeti.
newsitem.headline: Capital curbs worst case option -- Bnk Negara's Zeti.

text.p: Malaysia may consider capital controls as a worst case option to manage a crisis situation in excessive short term capital inflows, Bank Negara Assistant Governor Zeti Akhtar Aziz said on Monday.
But Zeti told Reuters the bank did not envisage a recurrence of such a crisis as seen in 1994, at least over the short-term.
"That is a crisis situation when the volume was so significant. So it would be used only under very unusual circumstances which we haven't seen since early 1994," she said.
"We do not envisage that we will see such massive flows because the situation is now completely different from the situation then...the macroeconomics we see and the financial conditions," she said.
Zeti earlier told a conference in Hong Kong Malaysia may consider capital controls as one possible option if short term capital inflows played too dominant a role in the banking system

"Bank Negara Malaysia would act pro-actively if it felt that short-term capital was playing too dominant a role in overall fund inflows into the country," conference sponsor I.D.E.A. said quoting Zeti.

Zeti also told the conference that the bank could use three options to confront capital inflows if the scenario presented itself -- allowing currency appreciation, increasing forex reserves and imposing capital controls.
Bank Negara last imposed capital controls in early 1994.

To curb what it said was "hot money" flowing into the country, it banned the sale of government paper to foreigners and imposed negative interest rates on foreign-held ringgit accounts, among other measures.
Zeti noted those measures were gradually removed in the course of the same year when the situation stabilised.
